1:
That the second son is called Daniel here and Chileab in Samuel is explained, not dismissed. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) rule out the easy answer on principle: the difference cannot well have arisen through an error of a copyist, and is probably to be explained by supposing the son had two different names. John Gill (reformed) says the same briefly, that he had two names. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) supplies two rabbinic reasons why, and they are not of a piece: the Targum has him called Chileab because he was in every respect like to his father, the word itself meaning like to the father; but Jarchi accounts for the double name from a doubt about his paternity, since David had taken Abigail immediately after Nabal’s death and it could not be ascertained whose son the child was, so that he was called Daniel, God is my judge, as well as Chileab. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) keeps to the wording, preferring a second, Daniel, to Abigail, noting that Samuel adds what this list omits, that she had been Nabal’s wife.

Whether Eglah was Michal divides them four ways. Gill reports without comment that the Targum makes her Michal, Saul’s daughter. Clarke reports the same from the Targum and Jarchi and then objects, that it does not well agree with the statement elsewhere that Michal had no child to the day of her death — though he leaves the door ajar, allowing she might have had a child before that time. Ellicott will not have it at all, calling the identification groundless, and explains the phrase his wife as added simply to balance the clause, making up for the absence of the details given for the other wives. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) takes that same phrase the opposite way, as marking her out: possibly she is so called because she was his first and therefore most proper wife, her son standing sixth only because he was born after the rest.

Bathsheba’s two names are read as a variant by one and a mistake by another. Gill observes that she is here called Bathshua and her father Ammiel where elsewhere he is Eliam, and treats them as names of much the same signification. Clarke makes it a copyist’s slip outright, one Hebrew letter having been put by mistake for another. He adds a point about the order of the list which the others do not raise, that Solomon is named last of the four although he was the eldest of them, because the genealogy was to be continued from him. Keil and Delitzsch simply count: thirteen more sons were born in Jerusalem, four of them Bathsheba’s, the names being enumerated again later in this book.

Ellicott notices a pun the rest pass over, that where the common Hebrew text reads to Absalom a number of manuscripts and all the old versions read simply Absalom, and that Kimchi takes the longer form as an allusion to a phrase meaning not Absalom — that is, no father of peace but a rebel. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads the list for its griefs rather than its names. David had many sons, and happy is the man that has his quiver full of such arrows; but some of them were a grief to him, Amnon and Absalom and Adonijah, and we do not read of any that imitated his piety or devotion except Solomon, who came far short of it. One of them he called Nathan, probably in honour of the prophet who had reproved him and been instrumental in bringing him to repentance, and it seems he loved him the better for it as long as he lived — from which Henry draws that it is wisdom to esteem those our best friends who deal faithfully with us.
8:
The count of David’s Jerusalem sons does not agree with Samuel, and the discrepancy is worked at. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) lays out the arithmetic, that there are thirteen if the four sons of Bathsheba are counted and nine without them, while Samuel gives eleven with those four and only seven without; and he resolves it by supposing that Samuel reckoned only those then living where the chronicler takes in the dead as well. He adds Jarchi’s alternative, that the duplicated names are what raise the regular seven to nine, and that the dead who left no posterity are named to swell the number of David’s descendants. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reaches the same solution more briefly, that two are omitted in Samuel because they died very early, whereas here we have all the sons of David. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) draws a different conclusion from the comparison, that the differences make it improbable these lists were drawn from the book of Samuel at all.

Ellicott alone explains why one of the names has shifted. The form meaning the Lord knoweth, which stands later in this book, he judges the more ancient, though Samuel also has the form meaning God knoweth; for God was of old called Baal as well as El, and the former title was discarded only because it tended to foster a confusion between the degrading cultus of the Canaanite Baals and the true religion of Israel. In later times, he says, men grew unwilling to write or even speak the name at all, and in compound names they substituted either El or Iah, as here, or else the word for shame, which is how Ishbosheth came to stand where an older form had Baal in it.

The concubines and the one named daughter are handled with some care. Ellicott observes that David’s concubines are mentioned several times in Samuel but their sons only here, and grants the difficulty plainly: however repugnant to modern ideas, it was and is part of the state of an Oriental potentate to possess a harem of many wives. Of Tamar he says she was not the only sister but the one whose unhappy fate had made her famous. Clarke puts the complementary fact, that she is the only daughter of David whose name is on record, although he is said elsewhere to have had both sons and daughters. John Gill (reformed) marks only the division of the list, that these were the sons by his wives, the concubines’ sons following.

On the line of kings the commentators pull in different directions. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads it for what it leaves out: David having nineteen sons, we may suppose them to have raised many noble families in Israel of whom we never hear, but scripture gives an account only of the descendants of Solomon here and of Nathan in the gospel — the rest had the honour to be sons of David, while these alone had the honour of relation to the Messiah, the sons of Nathan being his fathers as man and the sons of Solomon his predecessors as king. Ellicott works through the same names as a philologist, giving the sense of one after another, so that the succession shows itself to be almost wholly made up of names compounded with the divine name: the Kinsman has enlarged, Iah is father, Iah judgeth, Iah is high, Iah holdeth, Iah is strong, Iah helpeth, Iah is perfect, my strength is Iah — with Manasseh standing out as perhaps of Egyptian origin. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) simply carry the succession through to the sons of Josiah and then to the descendants of the captive and exiled Jeconiah. Gill marks where the reckoning changes, that from here to the end of the fourteenth verse the successors are given in the order of their reign.
17:
Three of them agree that Assir is no name at all. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) asks who Assir was and answers possibly nobody, since the Hebrew word signifies a prisoner and may be taken as an epithet of Jeconiah, who was a very long time prisoner in Babylon; Salathiel, he notes, was the son of Jeconiah, as the gospel genealogy has it. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reaches the same reading by two arguments of his own, that it accords with the Masoretic punctuation, which joins the word to Jeconiah, and that it accounts for the offspring of Jeconiah being mentioned twice over; he would render the clause, the sons of Jeconiah when captive, Shealtiel his son. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) glosses it the same way, of Jeconiah the captive, added to show that he begot his son while a prisoner in Babylon. On the prophecy that Jeconiah should be childless, John Gill (reformed) and Clarke both answer that it touches not his having children but his having none to succeed him in the kingdom, Clarke adding that the prophet interprets himself in saying no man of his seed shall prosper on the throne of David.

That Zerubbabel is called son of Pedaiah here and son of Shealtiel elsewhere produces four remedies. Gill will not take the easiest, declining the suggestion that this is a different Zerubbabel, and offers instead either that Pedaiah was himself a son of Salathiel so that Zerubbabel as grandson may be called his son, or rather that Salathiel, having no children, adopted his brother’s son and made him successor in the government. Clarke reports a bolder solution, that the words should simply be omitted, Pedaiah being wanting in the Syriac and Arabic, which would leave Zerubbabel the son of Salathiel as the gospel has him. Wesley takes the sentence to be short and imperfect, as is frequent in Hebrew, something being understood. Ellicott keeps the Hebrew as it stands, by which these six persons are sons of Jeconiah and brothers of Shealtiel, and notes only that Zerubbabel means born at Babel while his father is appropriately named, his name meaning Iah hath redeemed.

Where the text numbers six and names five, each offers a different way out. Clarke finds the versions no help and the manuscripts no correction, and concludes that either the father is counted with his sons or else a name has been lost out of the text. Wesley allows the first of those, including the father, but then suggests something none of the others consider, that the Hebrew word rendered six may itself be the proper name of one of the sons. Ellicott notes the same shortfall and looks to the versions, which at the preceding verse represent an important variant reading, the Greek turning what the Hebrew gives as several parallel families into a single descending line of son after son.

The list is also made to yield dates. Ellicott identifies one of the last names with the Hattush whom Ezra records going up with him in the second return, reckoning him of the fourth generation after Zerubbabel and so a likely youthful companion; and he places the sons at the very end of the chapter in the sixth generation from Zerubbabel, living under Artaxerxes Ochus — though he allows that if the Greek reading of the earlier verse is right their date falls four generations later. He finds the exile written into the names themselves, one of Jeconiah’s sons bearing a compound Babylonian name whose parts seem to mean that the moon-god should protect, such as might well be given to a Jewish prince at the court of Babylon, just as Daniel and his companions received idolatrous designations of the same sort. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) carry the lists through without comment to the descendants of the captive Jeconiah and the families that follow.
